title: How AI Is Rewriting the Economics of India's 15 Billion IT Industry
excerpt: Outcome-based contracts have doubled at TCS, clients demand 25–30% less for the same work, and mid-tier challengers are outpacing incumbents as the sector's biggest transformation in a generation accelerates.
body:
• Roughly 80% of BPO contracts at TCS are now outcome-based rather than billed by headcount — double the share since late 2023, according to CEO K. Krithivasan
  • India's Nifty IT index has lost more than 20% this year, erasing approximately $73 billion in market value as clients demand AI-augmented delivery at lower prices
  • Mid-tier challengers are outpacing large-cap incumbents: Persistent Systems posted 16% revenue growth and Coforge 33%, eating into Tier-1 market share
  • New contract structures are emerging where firms offer the first year free or split AI-generated savings with clients, fundamentally changing IT services economics

India's $315-billion IT services industry is undergoing its most significant structural transformation in a generation, as artificial intelligence rewrites the economics of outsourcing contracts, compresses deal sizes, and shifts competitive advantage away from scale and toward speed. A sweeping Reuters analysis draws on interviews with executives across the industry to map how the shift is playing out in real time.

The End of Headcount-Based Billing

The clearest signal of how fundamentally contracts are changing comes from TCS, India's largest IT exporter. CEO K. Krithivasan told Reuters that approximately 80% of the company's BPO contracts are now structured as outcome-based agreements, where payment is tied to measurable results rather than the number of employees deployed. That figure has roughly doubled since late 2023, reflecting a rapid industry-wide pivot driven by client demand.

The shift carries direct financial consequences. Outcome-based contracts transfer efficiency risk from the client to the service provider. When AI tools reduce the person-hours needed to deliver a given outcome, the savings accrue to the vendor only if it can cut costs faster than prices fall. When clients negotiate harder — as they increasingly are — the margin advantage erodes.

"We have seen clients on the application side demanding 25–30% less for the same work, and they're getting it."

— Persistent Systems executive, to Reuters

Shorter Deals, Harder Bargains

Contract durations are compressing alongside prices. Clients that once signed multi-year managed services agreements are increasingly opting for shorter engagements, retaining flexibility to renegotiate terms or switch vendors as AI capabilities improve. The trend puts additional pressure on revenue visibility — a metric that has traditionally underpinned IT company valuations.

Some firms are offering radically restructured deal terms to win business. HCLTech's engagement with E.ON, the European energy utility, reportedly includes a first year delivered at no charge — a loss-leader approach designed to lock in the client before AI-driven efficiencies generate returns in subsequent years. Cognizant's deal with Daimler reportedly splits AI-generated savings between the two companies, creating a shared-upside model that was virtually unheard of in traditional outsourcing.

Tech Mahindra CEO Mohit Joshi has publicly warned that some competitors are engaging in "irrational" pricing to secure deals, a sign that competitive intensity is rising as the revenue pool contracts.

Mid-Tier Challengers Gain Ground

While large-cap IT companies absorb the impact of pricing pressure on their massive delivery organizations, mid-tier firms are posting significantly stronger growth. Persistent Systems delivered 16% revenue growth in recent quarters, while Coforge expanded by 33%. Their smaller scale and higher exposure to digital-native client segments allow them to pivot delivery models faster and compete more effectively for AI implementation and consulting work.

The growth differential is reflected in brokerage ratings. Kotak Institutional Equities recently reversed its buy ratings on TCS and Infosys while maintaining preference for challengers — a shift that would have been nearly unthinkable two years ago when the Tier-1 companies were considered defensive safe havens.

TCS has laid off more than 12,000 employees so far in 2026 as it restructures delivery to align with AI-augmented workflows. Industry-wide workforce optimization is expected to continue, with automation absorbing an increasing share of tasks that were previously performed by entry-level engineers and BPO staff.

What It Means for the Industry

India's IT sector employs more than five million people and remains the single largest gateway for skilled Indian professionals to enter the global workforce, particularly through H-1B visas in the United States. The structural changes reshaping contract economics carry implications that extend well beyond quarterly earnings.

The Nifty IT index has lost more than 20% in 2026, following a 26% decline in 2025. The cumulative erosion of approximately $73 billion in market value reflects investor skepticism that AI-related revenue — from consulting, implementation, and platform modernization — can offset the deflation in traditional managed services and application maintenance.

For the industry's leadership, the challenge is existential in character if not yet in scale: how to deliver the same or better outcomes for clients with fewer people, shorter contracts, and compressed pricing, while retaining enough margin to invest in the AI capabilities that clients now expect as table stakes. The companies that solve that equation will define the next era of Indian IT. Those that do not will find themselves on the wrong side of the same disruption they are selling.
